messages.subject: basic function in ddply question
parts:
evening all

this strikes me as a simple application, but I can't figure what I'm doing wrong.

The question is as follows : I have observations of office holders over three successive committee ("comm" ) is the name of the committee variable. Officials ("official")are one of two parties (the variable is "party" and its two values are "r" and "d"). For each committee, I check to see if there are more "r" or more "d." Contingent on this answer, I rank order each official according to some other value ("g") either in ascending or descending order. I want a function which returns a data frame which reportss the 12th ranked official, for each committee. 

The data frame is 

foo <- data.frame(comm = rep(1:3, each = 20),
                         official = rep(1:20, times = 3),
                         party = sample(c("d", "r"), size= 60, replace = T),
                         g = runif(-1,1, n= 60))

and my attempt at the function I'll place inside ddply

offrank <- function(x) {
               ifelse(nrow(x[x$party == "d",]) >= nrow(x[x$party == "r",]),
                  i <- rank(x$g),
                  i <- rank(-x$g)
                  )
           j <- i[which(i == 12)]
           rm( i)
           }

ddply(foo, .(comm), offrank)

where I imagine I would would get a data frame listing committees and the 12th ranked official, but instead, I get told there's a data frame with no rows and no columns.

Since this is a pretty simple application, I'm sure I'm missing something fundamental. Sorry, and thanks in advance!

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: basic function in ddply question
parts:
Hi:

One problem with your function is that it doesn't return anything,
which is why you got the unexpected result. Here's an alternative
approach that's a little shorter:

offrank <- function(d) {
# make a table of party membership, coerce it to a numeric vector
v <- as.vector(table(d$party))
# orders by ascending g if v[1] >= v[2] (more d's) and descending o/w
u <- if(v[1] >= v[2]) d[order(d$g), ] else d[order(-d$g), ]
# grab the 12th row and return
tail(head(u, 12), 1)
}

> with(foo, table(comm, party))
party
comm d r
1 11 9
2 12 8
3 11 9

# => committee 2 should return the lowest ranking d, the other two the
highest ranking r
> ddply(foo, .(comm), offrank)
comm official party g
1 1 17 r 0.3068895
2 2 2 d 0.1550925
3 3 5 r -0.1013725

HTH,
Dennis

I'd recommend doing this in two steps. First compute the rank
variable and the subset based on that - that will make it much easier
to check your logic:

foo <- ddply(foo, "comm", mutate,
adjust = ifelse(mean(party == "d") > 0.5, 1, -1),
rank = rank(adjust * g)
)
subset(foo, rank == 12)

(I also used a slightly different approach to see which party was the biggest)

Hadley

messages.subject: Query on sub sampling with plyr or reshape2
parts:
Hi all,

I would like to extract random sub samples of critter occurrences over
time (per night) and compare with the entire nights worth of data.

The goal is to see if sub sampling will be adequate to determine species
presence.
Clearly sub samples will not be able to provide relative abundance but
may for 1/0 occurrence.

Given that some rare species are only present in small numbers my guess
is sub sampling may miss these.

Is there a way to use plyr or reshape2 to create repeated sub samples of
various data sets?
I am thinking sub samples would be some time period like 10 minutes at
the start of each hour or something like that.


Cheers from Gallon Jug,

Bruce

messages.author: 9ff02ee016b8a9e0
messages.subject: Re: Query on sub sampling with plyr or reshape2
parts:
Are you trying to return a data.frame, or something else?

One way to randomly sample is using the function sample.  Like:
sample(c(1,2,3), 1, replace=FALSE) # which will randomly choose a value from the vector you provide

Or randomly sample rows in a data.frame:
dat <- data.frame(label=seq(1,10,1), value=rnorm(10))
dat[ sample(NROW(dat), 5),  ]

Perhaps there is a solution that involves plyr or reshape2?

Scott Chamberlain
